anchor: Of Brownyis and of Bogillis
title: The epigraph from Gavin Douglas
short: From Gavin Douglas's Scots Eneados (1513), Prologue to Book VI: 'this book is full of brownies and bogles'.
body: Gavin Douglas (c. 1474-1522), Bishop of Dunkeld, translated Virgil's Aeneid into Scots; each book has an original prologue. In the Prologue to Book VI, which introduces Aeneas's descent to the underworld, he remarks that the book is full of brownies (household spirits) and bogles (goblins). Henley and Henderson note that the line should read 'Of browneis and of bogillis full this buke'. Prefixing it to a tale of a drunk farmer and a witches' dance is a mock-heroic joke: Tam's ride past Alloway Kirk is set beside Aeneas's journey to the dead.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh: T. C. & E. C. Jack, 1896), vol. I, text pp. 278-87 and notes pp. 433-41

anchor: When chapman billies leave the street
title: Occasion: Grose's Antiquities and Alloway Kirk
short: Written at Ellisland in 1790 to accompany a plate of Alloway Kirk in Francis Grose's Antiquities of Scotland, vol. II (1791).
body: Burns met the antiquary Francis Grose in 1789 and asked him to include Alloway Kirk, near his birthplace, in his survey; Grose agreed if Burns supplied a witch story. Burns first sent prose versions of three local legends, then, in December 1790, the poem. It was printed in Grose's volume in April 1791, and also appeared in the Edinburgh Herald and Edinburgh Magazine in March 1791; Bill Dawson argues that Grose's printing nonetheless has priority. Burns told Mrs Dunlop that it showed 'a finishing polish' he despaired of excelling. The opening paragraph, a general scene of market-day drinking, sets the comic, confiding voice of the narrator.

anchor: drouthy neibors
title: chapman billies ... drouthy neibors ... tak the gate
short: Pedlar fellows; thirsty neighbours; take the road home: the Scots vocabulary of market day.
body: A chapman is a travelling pedlar and 'billies' are fellows or comrades; 'drouthy' means thirsty, that is, fond of drink; 'to tak the gate' is to set off on the road ('gate' is the Scots word for way, from Old Norse gata). In the next lines 'bousing at the nappy' means drinking strong ale (nappy is ale with a head on it), 'fou' is drunk, and 'unco' is very. The narrator includes himself ('we sit bousing'), so the tale opens as fellow-feeling, not sermon.

anchor: her wrath to keep it warm
title: Nursing her wrath to keep it warm
short: The waiting wife broods over her anger like a fire tended at home: one of Burns's most quoted lines.
body: The wife at home is 'Gathering her brows like gathering storm', a simile that looks ahead to the real storm of the ride. The second line turns anger into something cherished and fed, like the fire the drinkers are sitting by. The couplet is comic and conventional (the shrewish wife of popular tales) but its precision has made it proverbial. Kate is not mocked for long, since the narrator later concedes she was right.

anchor: honest Tam o’ Shanter
title: Tam o' Shanter
short: Tam is named from Shanter farm on the Carrick shore; the hero is traditionally modelled on Douglas Graham (1739-1811).
body: Henley and Henderson report the tradition that Burns drew his hero from Douglas Graham, tenant of the farm of Shanter near Kirkoswald, a convivial man with a scolding wife, whose grey mare's tail was plucked by pranksters as she waited at a tavern door; Graham, so the story goes, blamed the witches of Alloway. 'Tam o' Shanter' means 'Tom of Shanter', the farmer being called by his farm's name in Scots fashion. 'Honest' is affectionate irony. The broad bonnet called a tam o' shanter takes its name from the poem.

anchor: thy ain wife Kate’s advice
title: Kate's warnings: skellum, blellum, melder
short: Kate called him a good-for-nothing and a babbling drunkard, sober on no market-day of the year.
body: Kate's catalogue of charges is given in Scots: a 'skellum' is a rascal, a 'blellum' an idle, babbling fellow; 'ilka melder wi' the Miller' means every time he took corn to be ground (a 'melder' is one load of grain ground at the mill), he sat drinking as long as he had 'siller' (money); 'ev'ry naig was ca'd a shoe on' means every time a nag was shod, he and the smith got 'roarin' fou'. She also accused him of drinking from Sunday to Monday with 'Kirkton Jean', probably Jean Kennedy, who kept a tavern at Kirkoswald with her sister (Henley and Henderson); 'the Lord's house' puns on church and inn. Her prophecy that he will drown in Doon or be caught by warlocks at Alloway Kirk sets up the plot. The passage is comic, but the narrator's next aside admits she was right.

anchor: Alloway’s auld, haunted kirk
title: Alloway's auld, haunted kirk
short: A ruined church near the Brig o' Doon, abandoned as a parish church since 1690 and close to Burns's birthplace.
body: The parish of Alloway was joined to Ayr in 1690, after which its church was left to fall into ruin; it stands a short way north of the Auld Brig o' Doon. Burns's father is buried in its kirkyard, and Burns was born in a cottage close by, so the place and its legends were familiar to him from childhood. He supplied Grose with witch stories attached to the kirk, and the poem makes it the scene of the Devil's dance.

anchor: Fast by an ingle, bleezing finely
title: ingle ... reaming saats ... Souter Johnie
short: By a blazing fireside, with foaming new ale, beside his crony the shoemaker.
body: 'Ingle' is a fire on the hearth; 'bleezing' is blazing. 'Reaming saats' (usually spelled 'swats') is foaming new ale, which 'drank divinely'. 'Souter' means shoemaker. Henley and Henderson note that a shoemaker named John Davidson (1728-1806) lived near Shanter and moved to Kirkoswald, and that he may lie behind the character, though they call the identification doubtful. The tavern scene is one of warmth, music and flirtation, the comic paradise before the storm.

anchor: But pleasures are like poppies spread
title: But pleasures are like poppies spread
short: A sudden shift into polished English: four similes for the brevity of pleasure.
body: The passage changes register from Scots narrative to the elegant English of Augustan moral verse. Pleasure is like a poppy whose bloom falls when it is picked, snow that falls on a river and melts at once, the aurora borealis that vanishes before one can point to it (the 'Borealis race', the darting northern lights), and a rainbow fading in a storm. The shift is partly parody of poetic moralising and partly genuine lyricism, and critics continue to debate how far the reader should take the lines seriously. Henley and Henderson defend the grammar of 'the snow falls in the river' against editors who emended it.

anchor: o’ night’s black arch the key-stane
title: night's black arch the key-stane
short: Midnight, the keystone at the top of the arch of night; the image foreshadows the keystone of the bridge.
body: The keystone is the central stone at the top of an arch. Midnight is the high point of the night's arch. The image is not idle: the ride will end at another keystone, that of the Brig o' Doon, where Tam reaches safety. The proverb 'Nae man can tether Time nor Tide' (time and tide wait for no man) marks the end of indulgence.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh: T. C. & E. C. Jack, 1896), vol. I, text pp. 278-87 and notes pp. 433-41

anchor: the chapman smoor’d
title: The haunted landmarks
short: Tam passes places of local death: a pedlar smothered in snow, a drunk who broke his neck, a murdered child, a suicide.
body: The paragraph is a grim catalogue: the ford where a chapman was 'smoor'd' (smothered) in snow, the birch trees ('birks') and big stone ('meikle stane') where drunken Charlie broke his neck, the gorse ('whins') and cairn where hunters found a murdered child ('bairn'), and the thorn tree above the well where Mungo's mother hanged herself. Each is a reminder of the fates Tam might share. The run of 'Where ... Where ... Where' builds suspense, and the Doon in flood and the lightning bring the scene to Kirk-Alloway 'in a bleeze' (ablaze).

anchor: Inspiring bold John Barleycorn!
title: John Barleycorn, tippenny, usquabae
short: John Barleycorn is malt liquor personified; 'tippenny' is twopenny ale, 'usquabae' whisky.
body: John Barleycorn is the hero of a traditional ballad (which Burns himself reworked) in which barley is 'killed', buried and crushed, and rises again as ale and spirits. 'Tippenny' is cheap ale sold at twopence the Scots pint; 'usquabae' is whisky, from Gaelic uisge beatha, 'water of life'. 'The swats sae ream'd in Tammie's noddle' (the ale so foamed in his head) that he did not care a 'boddle' (a small copper coin) for devils. The mock invocation treats drink as Tam's Muse and source of courage.

anchor: Nae cotillon, brent new frae France
title: The witches' dance and Auld Nick's piping
short: No fashionable French cotillion but Scottish hornpipes, jigs, strathspeys and reels, piped by the Devil as a shaggy dog.
body: The witches dance native Scottish dances, not the 'brent new' (brand-new) French cotillion of polite assemblies, a patriotic joke. In a 'winnock-bunker' (window-seat) sits Auld Nick, the Devil, 'in shape o' beast', a 'towzie tyke' (shaggy dog), who plays the bagpipes until roof and rafters 'dirl' (vibrate). Burns's prose letter to Grose also describes witches dancing round their 'old sooty blackguard master' and his bagpipe. Henley and Henderson record the first drafts of the coffin lines that follow.

anchor: To note upon the haly table
title: The horrors on the holy table
short: The altar bears a murderer's bones in gibbet-irons, unbaptised infants, a hanged thief, and weapons of murder.
body: The 'haly table' is the communion table, desecrated with relics of crime: bones in 'gibbet-airns' (the iron cage in which a hanged body was displayed), two tiny unbaptised babies, a thief just cut down from a 'rape' (rope), bloody tomahawks and scimitars, a garter used to strangle a baby, and a knife a son used on his father. The objects are lit by the corpses in open coffins 'like open presses' (cupboards), each holding a light by 'devilish cantraip sleight' (witchcraft). The list is gruesome and also absurd (the exotic tomahawks, the counting in fives), mixing gothic horror with comedy. Note that the archive's text reads 'his gabudid gape', a run-together misprint for 'his gab did gape' (his mouth gaped).

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh: T. C. & E. C. Jack, 1896), vol. I, text pp. 278-87 and notes pp. 433-41

anchor: even to name wad be unlawfu’
title: The four lines cut on Tytler's advice
short: An early version had four more lines after this one satirising lawyers and priests; Burns dropped them, reportedly at Tytler's request.
body: The omitted passage had three lawyers' tongues turned inside out, seamed with lies like a beggar's rag, and three priests' hearts, rotten and stinking, lying in every corner. A note on the manuscript by Alexander Fraser Tytler says Burns removed them at his request, as out of keeping with the pure horror of the scene. Some readers regret the cut, since the satire on professional hypocrisy sharpened the joke that the Devil's altar is little worse than the world's; others think the poem gains by not straying from Tam.

anchor: they cross’d, they cleekit
title: cleekit ... carlin ... swat and reekit
short: They linked arms; each old woman sweated and steamed, threw off her clothes and danced in her shift.
body: 'Cleekit' means hooked or linked arms (from 'cleek', a hook); 'carlin' is an old woman; she 'swat and reekit' (sweated and smoked with heat), 'coost her duddies' (cast off her rags) and 'linkit at it in her sark' (danced briskly in her shift). The archive's line reads 'The reel'd'; the authorised texts have 'They reel'd', which the sense needs. The rising tempo of the verbs imitates the accelerating dance.

anchor: Rigwoodie hags wad spean a foal
title: Rigwoodie hags wad spean a foal
short: Withered hags so ugly they would put a foal off its mother's milk; 'rigwoodie' is disputed.
body: 'Spean' means to wean, so the hags are hideous enough to wean a foal by fright. 'Rigwoodie' is a crux. Henley and Henderson explain that a rigwiddie is the rope or chain crossing a horse's saddle; some editors gloss the word as 'gallows-worthy' (from 'widdie', the gallows-rope); they themselves think it most probably means ancient or lean, since the simile concerns a mare. The narrator has just contrasted them with plump young 'queans' in 'snaw-white seventeen hunder linen', very fine linen woven, Henley and Henderson explain, in a reed of 1,700 divisions, for whose sight he would give his only breeches. 'Louping an' flinging on a crummock' means leaping and kicking on a crooked staff.

anchor: Her cutty sark, o’ Paisley harn
title: Nannie's cutty sark
short: The young witch Nannie dances in a 'cutty sark', a short shift of coarse Paisley linen bought when she was a girl.
body: 'Cutty' means short and 'sark' a shift or chemise; 'harn' is coarse linen, and Paisley was a centre of weaving. The garment, 'In longitude tho' sorely scanty', is the one her grandmother 'coft' (bought) for two pounds Scots, all her riches, never imagining it would grace a witches' dance. Nannie is 'waulie' (jolly, buxom) and 'vauntie' (proud of it). Burns's prose source has a farmer laughing at a witch whose smock was too short. The clipper ship Cutty Sark (1869) takes its name and figurehead from her.

anchor: my Muse her wing maun cour
title: my Muse her wing maun cour
short: A mock-epic invocation: the narrator's Muse must lower her wing, unable to describe Nannie's dancing.
body: 'Cour' means to lower or fold. The narrator pretends that the theme is too sublime for his powers, a standard epic topos (the poet's inadequacy before his subject) applied to a witch in a short shift. The device follows the Douglas epigraph and the Augustan similes in giving a local tale epic dress. Even Satan 'fidg'd fu' fain' (fidgeted with delight) and 'hotch'd' (jerked about) at the sight.

anchor: Weel done, Cutty-sark!
title: Weel done, Cutty-sark!
short: Tam loses his head and cheers aloud, and at once the lights go out and the witches pour out after him.
body: 'Tint his reason' means lost his reason (the archive's 'a thegither' should read 'a' thegither', altogether). The shout is the turning point: by speaking, Tam reveals himself, and the scene collapses into darkness. Burns's prose version has the farmer laugh 'Weel luppen, Maggy wi' the short sark!' (well leapt). The poem's climax thus comes from Tam's own unguarded delight, the same appetite that kept him at the tavern.

anchor: bees bizz out wi’ angry fyke
title: The chase similes
short: Three extended similes: angry bees from a raided nest, dogs after a hare, a crowd chasing a thief.
body: The witches pour out like bees ('bizz out wi' angry fyke', buzz out in a fuss) when boy-herds rob their 'byke' (nest), like the enemies of 'pussie' (the hare) when she starts up before them, like a market crowd at the cry 'Catch the thief!'. Extended similes are a feature of epic, and their use here continues the mock-heroic. Henley and Henderson explain the 'plundering herds' as herd-boys who robbed bumble-bees' nests. The witches' cry is 'eldritch' (unearthly).

anchor: running stream they dare na cross
title: the key-stone o' the brig
short: Witches and evil spirits cannot follow anyone past the middle of a running stream; Burns explained the belief in a note.
body: In the editions of 1793 and 1794 Burns noted that witches or evil spirits have no power to follow a poor wight any farther than the middle of the next running stream, and that turning back from bogles is more dangerous than going on. His prose letter to Grose calls this a 'universally known fact'. The keystone of the Brig o' Doon marks the midpoint of the river, so Meg must reach it to save Tam. The image fulfils the earlier description of midnight as 'night's black arch the key-stane', the keystone at the top of the arch of night.

anchor: left behind her ain grey tail
title: Maggie's tail
short: Meg's leap saves Tam, but Nannie seizes her tail and pulls it off: the comic price of escape.
body: 'Ettle' means intent or aim, 'claught' clutched, and 'the fient a tail she had to shake' means she had no tail at all left. The detail comes from local legend: in Burns's prose story the pursuing witch catches only the horse's tail, which gives way 'as if blasted by a stroke of lightning', and the tradition about Douglas Graham's plucked mare follows the same pattern. The hero escapes intact; his horse pays.

anchor: Remember Tam o’ Shanter’s mare
title: The moral
short: A mock-moral: beware drink and short shifts, lest you pay as dearly as Tam's mare.
body: The closing paragraph adopts the form of a cautionary ballad ('take heed') but its moral is comically inadequate: Tam has suffered nothing, his mare has lost her tail, and the warning lumps drink with lustful thoughts of 'Cutty-sarks'. Most readers see the ending as a final irony, in keeping with the narrator's earlier mock-solemnity; the poem celebrates the very pleasures it pretends to condemn.

sources.cite: W. E. Henley and T. F. Henderson, eds., The Poetry of Robert Burns (Centenary Edition, Edinburgh: T. C. & E. C. Jack, 1896), vol. I, text pp. 278-87 and notes pp. 433-41
'Tam o' Shanter (poem)', Wikipedia

anchor: tether Time nor Tide
title: Form and language
short: Octosyllabic couplets in the tradition of Butler's Hudibras, mixing Ayrshire Scots with passages of formal English.
body: The poem is in four-stress (octosyllabic) rhyming couplets, a metre associated in the eighteenth century with comic narrative, notably Samuel Butler's Hudibras. The language moves between broad Scots for action and dialogue and polished English for moralising and description, and the shifts are part of the comedy.
